read.sections.0.text.source: Many animals can learn, and some even use simple tools. But humans are especially good at sharing what they learn, because we use language to explain ideas in detail. A child can learn a skill from an older person, improve it and then teach it to others. In this way, knowledge can grow from one generation to the next. Some historians call this collective learning. For example, one person might find a better way to shape a stone tool. Others copy the idea, change it a little and pass it on, so it is not lost when one person stops using it.
read.sections.0.text.back: Many animals can learn, and some can even use simple tools. But humans are especially good at sharing what they have learned, because we use language to explain ideas in detail. A child learns a skill from an adult, makes that skill better, and then can teach it to others. In this way knowledge grows from one generation to the next. Some historians call this collective learning. For example, one person might find a better way to shape a stone tool. Others copy the idea, change it a little, and pass it on. So the idea doesn't disappear when one person stops using it.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Many animals learn. Some even use tools. But humans are very good at sharing what they learn. We use words to explain ideas. A child learns a skill from an older person. Then the child makes it better. Later, the child teaches others. So knowledge grows from one generation to the next. This is called collective learning. A good idea does not end with one person.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Many animals can learn. Some even use tools. But humans are very good at sharing what they learn. We use words to explain ideas. A child learns a skill from an adult. Then the child makes the skill better. Later the child teaches others. So knowledge grows from one generation to the next. This is called collective learning. Good ideas don't end with one person.

read.sections.1.text.note: Blombos Cave is ถ้ำบลอมโบส and Muna Island is เกาะมูนา (Thai transliterations, also in the picture); Sulawesi is สุลาเวสี (KEY_TERMS). The checker warns that the Latin names do not appear; that is expected for real places.
read.sections.1.text.source: Early humans did not leave any written records, so how do we know about them? An archaeologist studies the things that people left behind, such as tools, bones, footprints, fireplaces and art. A worn tool can show how people used it. Burned seeds in a hearth can show what people cooked. Art shows that people used signs and symbols. In Blombos Cave in South Africa, someone cut a neat pattern into a piece of red rock about 75,000 years ago. However, one object rarely proves a whole story, so archaeologists compare many finds from different places and times.
read.sections.1.text.back: Early humans left no written records at all. So how do we know about them? Archaeologists study what people left behind, such as tools, bones, footprints, hearths and art. A worn tool can tell how people used it. Burnt seeds in a hearth can tell what food people cooked. Art shows that people used marks and symbols. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, someone carved an ordered pattern onto a piece of red stone about 75,000 years ago. But one object almost never proves the whole story. So archaeologists compare many finds from many places and many periods.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Early humans did not write. So how do we learn about them? An archaeologist studies things that people left behind. Tools, bones and art are all clues. A worn tool shows how people used it. Burned seeds in a hearth show what people cooked. In South Africa, people marked a red rock with lines. That was about 75,000 years ago. But one object does not tell the whole story. So archaeologists look at many finds.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Early humans didn't write. So how can we know about them? Archaeologists study what people left behind. Tools, bones and art are all clues. A worn tool tells how people used it. Burnt seeds in a hearth tell what food people cooked. In South Africa, someone scratched lines onto a red stone. That was about 75,000 years ago. But one object doesn't tell the whole story. So archaeologists look at many finds.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Moving and adapting to new places
read.sections.2.heading.back: Travelling and adapting to new places

read.sections.2.text.note: "our species" is มนุษย์สายพันธุ์ของเรา; check (เผ่าพันธุ์ is another option but can suggest race).
read.sections.2.text.source: Scientists explain that our species first lived in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Over many thousands of years, groups slowly spread into Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas. This did not happen in one long trip. It happened a little at a time, over many generations. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and seasons, and they made new tools and clothes. To reach Australia, people had to cross the sea, so they must have built boats. A tool may look simple, but making it took planning, skill and teaching.
read.sections.2.text.back: Scientists explain that our human species first lived in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Over thousands of years, groups slowly spread to Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas. This didn't happen in one long journey; it happened little by little over many generations. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and seasons, and made new kinds of tools and clothes. To reach Australia, people had to cross the sea, so they must have built boats. One tool may look simple, but making it needed planning, skill and teaching.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Scientists say our kind of human first lived in Africa. That was about 300,000 years ago. Slowly, groups spread to other parts of the world. This took many thousands of years. It did not happen in one trip. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and weather. To reach Australia, they crossed the sea in boats. A tool may look simple. But making it took skill and teaching.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Scientists say humans like us first lived in Africa. That was about 300,000 years ago. Groups slowly spread to other parts of the world. It took thousands of years. It didn't happen in one journey. In each new place, people had to adapt. They learned about new plants, animals and weather. To reach Australia, they crossed the sea by boat. A tool may look simple, but making a tool needs skill and teaching.

write.example.source: The clues suggest that early humans learned skills from each other. Clue 4 shows tools with the same shape at sites far apart. This may mean that people copied a good design and taught it to others. Another clue is the hearth with layers of ash. People may have used the same fireplace many times and shared what they knew about fire and food. Together, these clues suggest collective learning. But the clues cannot tell us what words people used or who made the first tool.
write.example.back: The clues suggest early humans learned skills from each other. Clue 4 shows tools with the same shape at sites far apart. This might mean people copied good designs and taught them to others. Another clue is a hearth with many layers of ash. People may have used the same fireplace many times and shared what they knew about fire and food. Looking at these clues together suggests there was collective learning. But the clues can't tell us what words people used, or who made the first tool.

watch.summary.source: This video explains collective learning. Humans can use language to share ideas in great detail. So one person does not have to learn everything alone. Each generation can learn what older people knew and then add new ideas. Over time, knowledge grows. Early humans shared ways to find food, make tools, use fire and build shelter. This helped groups adapt to many different places, from hot lands to cold ones. We cannot hear what early people said. But tools slowly got better over time. This is a clue that people learned from each other. Collective learning did not make every group the same. Each community used what it knew in its own way, to fit its own place.
watch.summary.back: This video explains collective learning. Humans can use language to share ideas in great detail, so one person doesn't have to learn everything alone. Each generation learns what the generation before knew, then can add new ideas. Over time, knowledge grows. Early humans shared ways to find food, make tools, use fire and build shelters. This helped groups adapt to many very different places, from hot lands to cold lands. We can't hear what early people said, but tools slowly got better over time. This is a clue that people learned from each other. Collective learning didn't make every group the same. Each community used what it knew in its own way, to suit its own place.
